lead: Physical memory is cut into fixed-size frames; each process is cut into pages of the same size. A page table maps each page to any free frame, so memory need not be contiguous. Because page size is a power of two, the hardware splits an address into page number and offset by bits. A small cache called the translation look-aside buffer (TLB) keeps recent translations, avoiding a second memory read on most accesses. Every phone app, database and cloud virtual machine uses this pair: paging gives flexible placement, and the TLB makes it fast.
prereq: You need 4.1 for logical versus physical addresses and 4.3 for why contiguous allocation fails.

sections.h3: Pages, frames and the address split

blocks.text: Physical memory is cut into fixed-size blocks called frames. A process is cut into blocks of the same size called pages. Page and frame sizes are equal and always a power of two, so the hardware can split a logical address by bits instead of dividing.
p = logical address ÷ page size (integer part); d = logical address mod page size; physical address = frame × page size + d
blocks.where: p is the page number, d is the offset inside the page, and frame is the frame number that the page table gives for page p.

blocks.text: With page size 4 KB = 4096 bytes and a 32-bit logical address, the offset needs d = log₂ 4096 = 12 bits. The page number gets the remaining p = 32 − 12 = 20 bits.
Logical address 8196 = 2 × 4096 + 4, so page number p = 2 and offset d = 4. Each process has a page table with one entry per page. Entry 2 says frame 5. Physical address = 5 × 4096 + 4 = 20484.

The page-table base register (PTBR) holds the physical address of the page table; some syllabi call it the page-table pointer. Pages need not be contiguous, so any page can go in any free frame. Only the last page of a process may waste space inside its frame; this waste is internal fragmentation.

sections.h3: Why a TLB, and effective access time

blocks.text: Without a TLB every memory access costs two reads: one for the page-table entry and one for the data. The translation look-aside buffer (TLB) is a small, fast, associative memory inside the CPU. It caches recent page-table entries.

items: On a hit, the frame number is available at once and the access needs one memory read.
On a miss, the CPU reads the page table, then the data, and copies the entry into the TLB.
An address-space identifier (ASID) in each TLB entry tells which process the entry belongs to, so a context switch need not flush everything.
Some entries are wired: they cannot be evicted, and the kernel uses them for code that must never fault.

blocks.where: h is the hit ratio (0 to 1), t is the TLB search time in ns, m is one memory access time in ns, and EAT is the effective access time in ns.

blocks.text: Take h = 0.8, t = 10 ns and m = 100 ns. EAT = 0.8 × (10 + 100) + 0.2 × (10 + 100 + 100) = 88 + 42 = 130 ns. The miss case has two memory reads, not one.

A larger page means fewer page-table entries and fewer TLB misses, but more waste in the last page of each process. A smaller page wastes less, but the table grows and the TLB holds fewer useful translations. The operating system picks a size that balances table size, TLB reach and fragmentation.

The page table itself lives in memory, so the PTBR changes on every context switch. On a TLB miss the hardware reads the entry at PTBR + p × entry size. A page-table entry usually also stores valid, protection and dirty bits; those bits are checked during translation.

spec.aria: Logical address 8196 splits into page 2 and offset 4, the page table maps page 2 to frame 5, and the physical address becomes 20484.

examples.question: A system has 32-bit logical addresses and a page size of 4 KB. (a) How many bits are used for the page number and the offset? (b) Translate logical address 8196 when the page table says page 2 is in frame 5. (c) Find the effective access time if the TLB hit ratio is 0.8, TLB search takes 10 ns and a memory access takes 100 ns.
steps: Page size = 4 KB = 4096 = 2¹² bytes, so offset bits d = log₂ 4096 = 12 bits.
8196 ÷ 4096 = 2 with remainder 4, so page number p = 2 and offset d = 4.
examples.answer: Offset bits = 12, page-number bits = 20, physical address = 20484, and EAT = 130 ns.
examples.check:
page_size = 4096
logical = 8196
d_bits = 12
p_bits = 20
p = logical // page_size
d = logical % page_size
frame = 5
physical = frame * page_size + d
h = 0.8
t = 10
m = 100
eat = h * (t + m) + (1 - h) * (t + 2 * m)
print(d_bits)
print(p_bits)
print(p)
print(d)
print(physical)
print(eat)

traps: Do not compute offset bits as log₂(number of pages). It is log₂(page size in bytes).
EAT on a TLB miss includes the TLB search plus two memory reads: one for the page-table entry and one for the data.
A page is a logical unit and a frame is a physical unit; do not say a process is divided into frames.
Internal fragmentation occurs only in the last page of a process, not in every page.
The PTBR stores the physical address of the page table, not the page number of the current page.

quiz.a: A small, fast, associative cache inside the CPU that holds recent page-table entries.

quiz.q: Why does a memory access need two reads when there is no TLB?
quiz.a: One read fetches the page-table entry to find the frame, and the second read fetches the actual data from that frame.

quiz.q: Page size is 2 KB. Logical address 5000 maps to frame 7. Find the page number, offset and physical address.
Why does a TLB entry need an ASID?
quiz.a: Two processes can use the same page numbers for different frames. The ASID tells which process an entry belongs to, so a context switch need not flush the TLB.

quiz.q: How many offset bits does an 8 KB page need?
Why must page size be a power of two?
quiz.a: Then the address splits into page number and offset by bit positions, with no division in the hardware.

quiz.q: TLB hit ratio 0.9, TLB search 5 ns, memory access 80 ns. Find EAT.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real CPUs use a two-level TLB and a page-walk cache, and huge pages reduce TLB pressure in databases and virtual machines. Search next for TLB shootdown, ASID, huge pages, and page-walk cache.
